samples.summary: Image fetch/embed failures are now silently swallowed, so a browser PDF/DOCX export drops content with no user-visible signal and no failure
samples.evidence: `collectAndEmbedImages` wraps the whole per-src body in `try { ... } catch (error) { onImageError(src, error) }`, whose default `warnImageError` only calls `console.warn`; `pdf-painter.ts:680` then does `if (!entry) return;`. `DocxExporter.collectImages` (docx-exporter.ts:448-455) does the same, pushing `{rId:''}` so `inlineToXml` emits no run. Both exporters are used by the browser (`packages/frontend/src/app/docs/pdf-actions.ts:30`, `docx-actions.ts:50`) whose `docsImageFetcher` throws on any non-OK response (`export-utils.ts:52`) — a transient 401/network blip previously failed the export loudly; now the user downloads a PDF/DOCX silently missing images, with only a console.warn. On the CLI the export likewise completes with exit code 0 and no structured error envelope, so an agent cannot tell content was dropped. `packages/cli/src/docs/pdf-export.ts:39` still documents the old contract ("throws otherwise to avoid silently dropping content"), now stale.

samples.summary: `pinnedUrl` dials only `addresses[0]`, discarding fetch's multi-address (happy-eyeballs) fallback — http image fetches can fail on hosts whose first record is unreachable
samples.evidence: `const address = addresses[0]; url.hostname = ...` uses the first record from `dnsLookup(hostname, { all: true, verbatim: true })`. `verbatim: true` preserves resolver order, which for a dual-stack CDN commonly puts the AAAA record first. On a machine without working IPv6 (or when the first A record is down), the normal `fetch(name)` path would try the remaining addresses; the pinned URL cannot, so the connection fails and — combined with the new swallow in the exporters — the image is silently dropped from the export. No fallback loop over the other approved addresses exists.

samples.summary: The new catch is wider than the fetch it was added for: decode/embed errors are swallowed too
samples.evidence: The `try` at line 81 spans `fetcher(src)`, `blob.arrayBuffer()`, `pdfDoc.embedPng/embedJpg`, and `embedAsPng`. The doc comment justifies the catch by "fetch refused, host unreachable", but a corrupt PNG (`embedPng` throw) or the explicit Node/jsdom `Image format ... requires a DOM Canvas to convert` error (line 142) — which the tests at `pdf-exporter.test.ts` previously relied on surfacing — are now downgraded to a console.warn as well, hiding genuine exporter bugs.

samples.summary: `AbortSignal.timeout` also bounds body streaming, so a large-but-legal image on a slow link is aborted mid-read and dropped
samples.evidence: `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs)` is passed to `fetchImpl`, and the signal stays live while `readCappedBlob` drains `res.body`. A 25 MB image (exactly the documented cap) on a link slower than ~0.9 MB/s exceeds the 30 s default before the body finishes, so `reader.read()` rejects with AbortError and the image is dropped. The timeout is documented as protecting against a host that "accepts the connection and then never answers", i.e. it was intended as a response-headers timeout, not a whole-transfer budget.

samples.summary: The `host` header used to preserve virtual-host routing on a pinned request may be ignored, sending `Host: <ip>` instead
samples.evidence: `{ headers: { host: new URL(current).host } }` — `host` is a forbidden header name in the fetch spec; whether it survives depends entirely on the runtime's `Headers` guard implementation. If it is dropped, every pinned `http:` request arrives at the IP with `Host: <address>`, so name-based virtual hosts / CDN edges return the wrong site or a 404 and the image is (now silently) dropped. Nothing in the code detects or falls back from this; the only coverage is a stub fetch that echoes whatever init it was handed.

samples.summary: `upstreamErrorJson` is reached on a successful-but-empty download, reporting a misleading `HTTP 200` error
samples.evidence: `if (!res.ok || !res.bytes) { io.stderr(upstreamErrorJson(res)); return { exitCode: 1 }; }` — when the server answers 200 with a zero-length/absent body, `res.ok` is true and `res.status` is 200, so `upstreamMessage` produces `{ error: { code: 'HTTP_ERROR', message: 'HTTP 200' } }`, which tells the caller nothing about the actual condition (empty payload).
